Exercising regularly can improve your strength, mobility, fitness level, energy, and mood when living with MS, but how much you can do depends entirely on what works for you and your current abilities. Your physician or physical therapist is best equipped to suggest an exercise routine that meets your needs, so make sure to consult with them first to get a clear recommendation specific to your condition.

In general, though, the National Multiple Sclerosis Society recommends incorporating aerobic exercises, strengthening exercises, and stretching or range-of-motion exercises into your routine. Aerobic activities can include swimming, walking, and using a stationary bike. Strength training exercises, like working with resistance bands or free weights, and stretching can help maintain and increase muscle strength and flexibility. Gentle yoga, pilates, or tai chi might be good options to consider for these kinds of exercise as well.

Listen to your body. It's okay to take frequent breaks, slow down, switch to a shorter or easier routine, or even rest for some days if you're not up to it. Avoid overheating and dehydration during physical activity, too, since they can temporarily worsen symptoms. If you experience any new or increased disability after exercising, check with your doctor before resuming your workout routine.

Lastly, consider joining a local or online support group focused on wellness with MS; members who have faced similar issues can share their experiences and advice on exercise as a way to help you feel more comfortable starting out.

5. **Balance Training**: Simple balance activities like side lunges, toe stands, and tandem walking can reduce the risk of falls.

Before beginning any fitness routine, discuss your plans with your healthcare provider to avoid pushing yourself too hard when symptoms worsen, which may be more likely during hot weather or illness.
